summary: For ages 7–9: understand that tropical rainforests are consistently hot (about 25–30°C) and very wet (over 2000 mm rain/year) all year, with little seasonal change, and that it is the COMBINATION of constant heat AND constant moisture — not heat alone — that drives rapid plant growth and extraordinary biodiversity. Learners quantify 'hot and wet' with real numbers, compare the rainforest with their own climate and with a hot desert, and distinguish weather (today) from climate (the usual multi-year pattern).
misconceptions: 'Rainforests have a hot season and a cold season like us' — they are hot and wet consistently, with little seasonal change.
'Hot places are all like deserts' — deserts are hot but DRY; it's the added water that makes rainforest life.
'Weather and climate are the same' — weather is today; climate is the long-term usual pattern.
'It only rains sometimes' — rainforests receive very high rainfall spread through the year.
'Any warmth makes a rainforest' — without high rainfall you get grassland or desert, not rainforest.

activities.title: Two dials: heat and water together
steps: Start with a bare patch of ground shown on screen or on paper, controlled by two settings: TEMPERATURE and RAINFALL.
Set temperature high but rainfall low, and describe/predict what the patch becomes (hot but dry → cracked desert, little life such as a lone cactus).

Set rainfall high but temperature low, and describe the result (cool and wet → slower growth and fewer kinds of plants and animals, e.g. mosses and ferns on a cold, wet hillside; real cool, wet places can still be green, but they have much less variety of life than a tropical rainforest).
Set BOTH high to tropical values (about 28°C, soaking wet, all year) and describe the result (towering trees, vines, many animals, a 'growth/biodiversity' meter near maximum).
Jump between preset settings for 'Rainforest/Amazon', 'UK' (cool, moderate rain, modest life) and 'Desert' (hot, dry) and compare the amount of life in each.
State in your own words the rule you discover: it is heat AND water held high together, all year with no off-season, that produces the most crowded, fastest-growing habitat.
activities.insight: Rainforest lushness comes from constant heat AND constant heavy rain combined; either variable alone (hot desert, or cool wet hillside) gives a very different, much less biodiverse place.

activities.title: Three-way climate compare with real numbers
steps: Read or build a compare of three places — tropical rainforest, the UK (or your local area), and a hot desert — showing temperature and rainfall for each.

Record the numeric anchors: rainforest ~25–30°C and >2000 mm rain/year; note the UK as cooler, with less rain in most places (about 600–1200 mm/year in many areas, though some western hills get more) and clear seasons; note the desert as hot but very dry (often under 250 mm/year).
For each place, note how much life it supports and link it back to its temperature and rainfall.
Answer: which single factor most separates the rainforest from the desert? (water); and what are the main differences from the UK? (constant heat, much more rain, and no cold season).
Write one or two sentences explaining why the rainforest's figures produce fast year-round growth.
activities.insight: 'Hot and wet' becomes quantified and comparative: learners can say roughly how much hotter and wetter a rainforest is than their own climate and than a desert, and why those numbers matter.

activities.title: Weather today vs climate over years
steps: Compare a 'today's weather' statement (e.g. 'it is raining right now') with a 'climate' statement (e.g. 'it is hot and wet most of the year, every year').
Sort several example statements into 'weather (today)' or 'climate (usual long-term pattern)'.
Explain why a rainforest can have a rainy day and a drier day but still be described as hot and wet all year.
State that the rainforest climate has little seasonal change — unlike the UK's distinct seasons — so there is no cold season, and usually no long dry season, to stop plant growth.
activities.insight: Weather is what is happening now; climate is the usual pattern over many years. The rainforest's climate is consistently hot and wet with little seasonal variation, which is why plants can keep growing all year round.

activities.title: Explain the Sahara-vs-rainforest puzzle
steps: Consider: the Sahara desert is hot; a rainforest is also hot — yet one has very little visible life and the other bursts with plants and animals.
State the difference in their climate (the desert is hot but dry; the rainforest is hot AND very wet).
Then explain WHY that difference matters so much (constant heat plus abundant water lets plants grow fast all year, supporting huge biodiversity; heat alone without water gives a desert).
Answer follow-up prompts: roughly how much more rain does a rainforest get than where you live? Does a rainforest have a cold winter? What would a hot place with almost no rain become?
activities.insight: The learner can independently articulate that rainfall is the key difference and that it is the heat-and-water combination that produces rapid growth and biodiversity.

checkQuestion: The Sahara desert is hot. A rainforest is also hot. Both are hot places — so why does one become a lifeless-looking desert and the other burst with plants and animals? Tell me the difference in their climate, and then tell me WHY that difference matters so much.
checkAnswer: The difference is water. The rainforest is hot AND very wet — over 2000 mm of rain a year and warm (25–30°C) all year — while the desert is hot but dry. It's the COMBINATION of constant heat and constant heavy rain that lets plants grow fast all year and supports so much life. Heat alone (as in a desert) isn't enough; without the water you get a desert, not a rainforest.
